title: How the Dark Side Seahawks defense shut down Fernando Mendoza, Raiders in the Death Star
content:
LAS VEGAS — The Seattle Seahawks spoiled Fernando Mendoza’s starting debut, beating the Las Vegas Raiders 21-13 at Allegiant Stadium on Sunday.

The defending Super Bowl champions came alive in the second half, erasing a 10-7 halftime deficit with a 9-yard touchdown run from Jadarian Price and adding to it with a 71-yard scoring reception by Jaxon Smith-Njigba in a decisive third quarter.

Mendoza, the No. 1 pick in April’s NFL Draft, got the Raiders out to a 10-7 halftime lead, scoring on a 10-yard run to cap an 11-play first-quarter drive. But Seattle’s defense stiffened in the second half, finding answers for Mendoza and the Raiders.

The Seahawks moved to 6-4. They’re on bye next week, then go on the road to play the NFC West-leading 49ers in Week 12. The Raiders fell to 4-6 and will face the Broncos in Denver next week.

Box score | Week 10 blog | Game discussion

Mendoza passed with flying colors in the first half. He got the ball on a short field after a fumble by Drew Lock for his first drive and used the advantage masterfully: a perfect 3-for-3 passing and rushing for a 10-yard score on a third-down quarterback draw. He looked strong on his second drive, too, using his legs to convert a third down and completing four passes on a drive that ended with a field goal. Mendoza went into the break 11-for-13 passing for 90 yards, adding five carries for 21 yards and the touchdown.

But the poise paled after halftime. He succumbed to several sacks on third-and-longs. The pressure affected several of the throws he got off. He was just 17 for 29 for 143 yards, as the Raiders punted on five straight drives coming out of the break.

Mendoza’s mobility looked to add something different to the Raiders offense to start. But as he hung in the pocket trying to dissect one of the league’s most shape-shifting defenses in the second half, he struggled. It also didn’t help that he lost his top target, Brock Bowers, to an ankle injury after the game’s first two drives.

Overall, I’d give Mendoza a solid B. The potential is clear — his partnership with head coach Klint Kubiak could be something special when all is right. But he couldn’t persevere when it wasn’t. Mendoza faces another tough defense with a trip to Denver next week — it will be interesting to see how he adjusts. — Sam Warren, Raiders beat writer

While Seattle’s injured offensive line didn’t exactly help running back Zach Charbonnet, the fourth-year running back continues to impress in his return from tearing his ACL in the playoffs last January.

Charbonnet, who made his season debut two weeks ago against the Chicago Bears, had his most productive game this year, rushing for 94 yards on 20 carries.

There have been few, if any, signs of Charbonnet’s knee limiting him. The tailback, who is more typically known for his bruising style, was evasive in the open field, flashing both burst and agility to leave would-be Raiders tacklers in the dust.

As much as Seattle’s rushing attack struggled while Charbonnet missed the first half of the season, he has come back into the fold to inject some much-needed life into Seattle’s offense at an opportune time.

The Seahawks are still reliant on Smith-Njigba, who had an outstanding second half. But this offense functions best when it can churn out yards on the ground. That’s precisely what Charbonnet did all afternoon. – Andrew Destin, Seahawks beat writer

Short answer: Jaxson Smith-Njigba happened. The Seahawks’ star receiver had just two targets in the first half. In the third quarter alone, he had six catches for 144 yards and a touchdown. Smith-Njigba took advantage of the Raiders’ rookie defensive backs on the first drive out of the break, beating corners Hezekiah Masses and Jermod McCoy for a pair of chunk plays to set up a Jadarian Price touchdown. Offensive coordinator Brian Fleury then found a way to get him matched up against linebacker Quay Walker – an assignment the Raiders never wanted to occur – and Smith-Njigba won easily over the top, taking in a 71-yard score.

The Raiders limited Smith-Njigba’s involvement early with timely stops on defense and help from the offense. They forced Lock to fumble on their first drive, and then got a third-down stop on their third. Mendoza also had Las Vegas sustaining drives early, keeping the Seahawks offense off the field.

But with a bunch of short possessions to come, the struggles that have plagued the Raiders defense through the season’s first half arose yet again. They were gashed on the ground, setting up deep shots against outmatched defenders downfield. This group needs turnovers and offensive help to be effective. They got that to start, but their deficiencies showed as the game wore on. – Warren

Through the game’s first two quarters, it appeared the Raiders had figured out a way to slow down the NFL’s leading receiver in a way that no other team has this season. Smith-Njigba, who was held to a season-low 51 receiving yards in last week’s 17-3 win against the Arizona Cardinals, had only one reception for 11 yards on two targets in the first half.

It was a much different story in the third and fourth quarters.

Seattle opened up the offense in the second half, and reaped the benefits of that approach. Not only did Smith-Njigba haul in a 71-yard touchdown reception on a play in which he slipped past the last lines of the Raiders’ defense, but he also had six more passes for 89 yards finish with his most receiving yards (171) in a game this season.

Smith-Njigba’s first-half opportunities were limited, both because Seattle couldn’t stay on the field and Lock didn’t attempt that many passes. Once the Seahawks found their rhythm on offense, though, the Raiders’ leaky pass defense didn’t have much of a shot at containing Smith-Njigba. – Destin

Seattle entered Sunday’s game without its starting left tackle, Charles Cross, as well as recently acquired left guard, Quenton Nelson, both of whom are out with injuries. The offensive line became further banged up when right tackle Abe Lucas went down with an ankle injury in the second quarter after Lock rolled into him on a sack.

Though reserve Bobby Hart, who has 109 games of NFL experience, including 75 starts, filled in for Lucas, he’s spent most of this season on Seattle’s practice squad for a reason.

Last season, the Seahawks’ offensive line improved as the season progressed, and Seattle became increasingly effective at running the ball. Without three projected starters, though, the Seahawks are struggling in the trenches, and their offense was significantly hampered as a result.

In the first half, Seattle possessed the ball for just 10:45 and converted only four first downs. While Charbonnet averaged 4.9 yards per rush before halftime, more than half that output came on one 24-yard scamper.

Otherwise, there were few holes for Charbonnet and rookie running back Jadarian Price to run through in the first half. – Destin
